          PART 1     WINTERIZATION REQUIREMENTS
          1.1    Each Submission must comply with the following requirements:
             A. The Facility must comply with applicable EOP-012-1 (Extreme Cold Weather Preparedness and
             Operations) requirements, including Requirements R1 (applicable to New Facilities), R2 (applicable to Existing
             Facilities), R3, R4, R5, R6, and R7. EOP-012-1 (Extreme Cold Weather Preparedness and Operations) is
             published by NERC and available at: https://www.nerc.com/pa/Stand/Reliability%20Standards/EOP-012-1.pdf.
             B. Bidder must provide, by no later than Bid Due Date, the Facility’s: (i) extreme cold weather temperature; and
             (ii) cold weather preparedness plan.
          PART 2     CYBERSECURITY
          2.1    Each Facility must comply with the requirements for Bulk Electric System generation facilities in North
          America set forth in the NERC reliability standards (Cyber Security Standards) created pursuant to FERC order
          706 (Mandatory Reliability Standards for Critical Infrastructure Protection) and any other cyber security best
          practices consistent with Prudent Industry Practices.
          2.2     All programmable electronic components of the (i) Battery Management System (“BMS”); (ii) BESS
          Controller; and (iii) Site Controller (including controls, hardware, and software) must not be sourced from or
          manufactured by Foreign Entities of Concern as defined in 42 U.S.C. § 18741(5) and subsequently interpreted in
          “Interpretation of Foreign Entity of Concern,” 89 Fed. Reg. 37085 (May 6, 2024) or sourced from or manufactured
          in one of the following countries: China, Russia, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Serbia, Algeria, Venezuela, Iran, Iraq,
          Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Syria, Lebanon, South Sudan, Pakistan, or Cuba. For purposes of
          this provision, the terms Battery Management System, BESS Controller, and Site Controller are defined as follows:
             A. Battery Management System (BMS): A control system used to protect the battery and to provide
             key parameters, such as state of charge, battery health, and temperature.
             B. BESS Controller: A controller used to manage multiple stacks or arrays of batteries. This controller
             manages the balancing of the batteries.
             C. Site Controller: A control system used to manage one or more sources (Photovoltaic solar,
             batteries, etc.) to achieve facility level control.
          PART 3     ADDITIONAL MINIMUM FACILITY TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR FACILITIES
          3.1    PPA Bids for a battery energy storage system (“BESS”) must meet the requirements set forth above in
          Sections 2.1 and 2.2 of this Exhibit O and the following requirements regarding the BESS:
             A. BESS
               (i) Units listed to UL9540 2nd edition.
               (ii) UL9540A large scale fire test report provided at the cell, module, and unit level.
               (iii) BESS complies with the version of NFPA 855 in effect at the time of Commercial Operation.
               (iv) A water connection and firefighting system shall be installed for responding to a thermal event.
               (v) Thermal Management System (TMS) design with redundancy and/or contingency for TMS component
               failure are required (e.g., redundant HVAC, fans, or ability to operate in derated condition with TMS
               component failure).
               (vi) Provide Site-specific Hazard Mitigation Analysis (HMA) and Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA).
               (vii) Provide detailed augmentation plan for the Facility over the PPA Term.
               (viii) BESS must be sized to maintain rated nameplate instantaneous Energy output capacity at the POI.
             B. Inverter
               (i) BESS inverters must be capable of operating full lead and lag in both charge and discharge conditions.
               (ii) BESS inverters must be grid forming capable. Bidders must provide documentation demonstrating the
               inverter’s grid forming capability.
               (iii) Inverter grid forming control points must be integrated into the Facility site control scheme, such that

          above in Sections 2.1 and 2.2 of this Exhibit O applicable to BESS:
             A. Hydrology and Site Drainage
               (i) Site grading must ensure positive drainage of the Site.
               (ii) Site design must ensure no flooding, no standing water, and no increase in flows offsite, as prescribed
               by the Georgia Stormwater Management Manual.
               (iii) The drainage design must be based on a 100-year, 24-hour rain event.
               (iv) No portion of the Facility will be located in a floodplain without the proper permit(s) from the appropriate
               Governmental Authority. GPC reserves the right to review the location of any portion of a Facility proposed
               to be in a floodplain, as well as any such permit(s).
               (v) The construction contract scope must include responsibility of contractor to close out the National
               Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit.
               (vi) Contractor will remain responsible for getting the Notice of Termination (NOT) verified and signed by
               the agency.
             B. Site Grading and Stabilization
               (i) Balanced earthwork is desired. Grades within the array to be used for vehicular/equipment ingress and
               egress must be no steeper than 10%. The maximum slope for areas of elevation transition must not exceed
               a ratio of 3:1.
               (ii) Measures must be in place to prevent sediment loss.
               (iii) Permanent site vegetation and site stabilization must be completed before Final Completion.
             C. Facility Design
               (i) Equipment must be sized to deliver rated Facility nameplate instantaneous energy output at the POI,
               accounting for worst-case local ambient temperature, plant losses (including auxiliary power), and
               interconnection reactive power requirement.
               (ii) Site performance at the POI must meet the interconnection requirements as set forth by the
               Interconnection Provider.
               (iii) Reactive power requirement must be solely met by the inverters without the use of capacitor banks.
               (iv) Input and output of all control and communication devices must be wired out to marshalling terminal
               blocks that is easily accessible.
               (v) All equipment enclosures (e.g., combiner boxes) must be tamperproof and lockable (e.g., a special tool
               or key is required to open the equipment enclosure).

            D. Major Equipment Vendors
              (i) Major equipment vendors must demonstrate quality and performance and be prepared to perform future
              warranty and maintenance work.
              (ii) Major equipment must be manufactured in factories certified to both IEC TS 62941 and ISO 9001.
              (iii) Final major equipment vendors subject to review and approval by GPC.
            E. Inverter
              (i) Inverters must be listed to UL1741 latest version.
              (ii) Inverters must be approved by GPC.
              (iii) Inverters must be capable of producing their maximum rated reactive power at all active power levels
              (from 0% to 100% inclusive), when the primary energy source is available and not available.
              (iv) Inverters must be equipped with DC ground detection means through either insulation monitoring or
              differential current monitoring.
              (v) A lockable fused disconnect must be provided at each discrete incoming DC input.
              (vi) Facilities that are transmission interconnected must conform to NERC recommendations and
              requirements pertaining to IBR facilities.
            F. Inverter Step-up Transformer
               (i) Transformers must be two-winding and KNAN type cooling; winding must be copper.
               (ii) Transformers must be equipped with fully rated no-load tap changers at HV side two taps at 2.5% above
               nominal position and two taps at 2.5% below nominal position must be provided.
               (iii) All transformers must be IEEE routinely tested including dielectric test, impulse test, and power factor
               test. Lightning impulse tests must include one full wave test.
               (iv) Two IR windows must be provided on both low side and high side terminations.
               (v) Oil reservoir for spill containment must be provided for each transformer.
            G. MV Switchgear
              (i) Outdoor rated metal-clad medium-voltage (MV) switchgear (e.g., over a sectionalizer cabinet) must be
              provided when required to combine and reduce the number of circuits to the substation; a main breaker must
              be provided.
              (ii) MV switchgear protection scheme must at minimum include main break protection, feeder breaker
              protection, bus differential protection, a dedicated bus lockout, and breaker failure functionality.
              (iii) All current transformers (CT) must have an accuracy class of C400 or higher.
              (iv) Bidder must coordinate with GPC on specific relays used and protection philosophy.
            H. Grounding
              (i) Dual grounding, as depicted in IEEE 665, must be provided in all cases with an equipment grounding
              conductor (for a reliable ground fault current return path) and an additional local safety ground (for limiting
              touch potential).
              (ii) Safety ground must be bare stranded copper #2/0 AWG or larger and direct buried, with risers bonded
              to each row of PV array and all equipment.
              (iii) Grounding study must be provided for the entire Site to determine the safety grounding design for
              limiting hazardous touch and step potentials during a worse case postulated ground fault event.
            I.    Cable Management
                 (i) All equipment enclosure within the PV array must be located at the end of PV racking rows towards the
                 road and facing the same direction whenever possible.
                 (ii) All DC wiring must be below grade unless routed along and below the PV array to prevent the blocking
                 of aisle space between rows. However, an E-W CAB system will be acceptable for Facilities with trackers.
                 All DC and LV AC cables below grade must be routed in conduit.
                 (iii) PV array must use single string harness that routes strings directly to the combiner box or the string
                 inverter. (i.e., harness that combines multiple strings must not be used).

              (iv) RIS-type bushings are preferred.

              (iii) The real time data must include inverters, solar details, MET station (if applicable), breakers, meters,
              and site controller. Solar details to pass data down to string or the lowest level possible.
              (iv) Site controller, battery management system (if applicable) and inverters time must be synchronized to
              a local time clock. The preference is to time sync with any devices that can take a remote time sync.
              (v) Local Human Machine Interface platform must be Ignition by Inductive Automation.
            N. Cyber Security
               (i) Equipment providers and site design must comply with NERC CIP policies as well as the Southern
               Company Cyber Security Policy, which will be made available to Bidders upon their submission of an intention

            O. End-of Life Disposal
              (i) The Toxicity Characteristic Leaching Procedure (TCLP) testing procedure and results for modules must

===== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-JKA-1 PD/STF-JKA-1-27.docx =====
STF-JKA-1-27

Question: 
How did Georgia Power address the Commission approved Stipulation/Order from the 2022 IRP, specifically regarding the following paragraphs. Also for each item below, explain how the Company modeled the resources in the Company’s Load and Resource Balance Table, and in Aurora:
a. Stipulation par. 19 – 2,100 MW of new utility scale renewable resources associated with the CARES program, greater than 6 MWs in size.
b. Stipulation par. 22 – Up to 200 MW of distributed generation solar resources between 250 kW and 6 MWs in size.
c. Stipulation par. 27 – The Community Solar Program.
d. Stipulation par. 33 – 250 MW pilot Demand Response Credit Tariff and the Resilience Asset Service Tariff.
e. Stipulation par. 35 – The Tall Wind demonstration project.
f. Commission Order par. 73 – Georgia Power’s acquisition of 500 MW of additional Energy Storage Systems via the Commission’s RFP bid process.
Response: 
See Chapter 2, “Implementation of Prior IRPs,” in the 2025 IRP Main Document for discussion regarding implementation of the 2022 IRP. 
The 2,100 MW of new utility scale renewable resources associated with the Clean and Renewable Energy Subscription (“CARES”) Program referenced in Stipulation para. 19 is shown in the Company’s Load and Resource Balance Table as “2022 IRP SOLAR US RFP 1” and “2022 IRP SOLAR US RFP 2”. In Aurora, the program is modeled as “O1_2022_IRP_US_RFP_1” and “O1_2022_IRP_US_RFP_2”.  The modeled nameplate capacity for the 2022 IRP SOLAR US RFP 1 was reduced to 50% from the 2023 IRP Update based on expected procurement challenges. See Chapter 8 Section 11.2 on Dynamic Procurement Challenges for Renewable Procurement of the 2025 IRP Main Document for more information.  Additionally, the first year of availability for both resources was delayed in the model. Based on market feedback, the RFP was modified to allow for RCODs as late as 2029. 
The distributed generation solar resources referenced in Stipulation para. 22 of the 2022 IRP are shown in the Company’s Load and Resource Balance Table as “2022 IRP SOLAR DG RFP 1” and “2022 IRP SOLAR DG RFP 2”. In Aurora, the program is modeled as “O1_2022_IRP_DG_RFP_1” and “O1_2022_IRP_DG_RFP_2”. 
The Customer Solar Program referenced in Stipulation para. 27 of the 2022 IRP is shown in the Company’s Load and Resource Balance Table as "Community Solar - Comer", "Community Solar - Guyton", and "Community Solar - Waynesboro". In Aurora, the program is modeled as “O1_COMMSOLAR_COMER”, “O1_COMMSOLAR_GUYTON”, and “O1_COMMSOLAR_WAYNESBORO”. 
The Demand Response Credit Tariff and the Resilience Asset Service Tariff pilot program referenced in Stipulation para. 33 is shown in the Company’s Load and Resource Balance Table under Dispatchable DSO Programs as “DER Customer Programs.” It is modeled as 0 MW of capacity because there are currently no active customers enrolled in the program.
The Tall Wind demonstration project referenced in Stipulation para. 35 was not modeled in the Load and Resource Balance Table or Aurora. As set forth in Paragraph 74 of the approved 2022 Order, the Commission did not approve the provision of the Stipulation for the tall wind demonstration project.  
The 500 MW of energy storage system (“ESS”) resources approved in the 2022 Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”) was for a request for proposals (“RFP”) to the market and is shown in the Company’s Load and Resource Balance Table as “2022 IRP ESS RFP” and modeled in Aurora as “O3_2022_IRP_ESS.”

===== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-JKA-1 PD/STF-JKA-1-4.docx =====
STF-JKA-1-4

Question: 
Regarding the Economically Optimal SERVM Reserve Margin Study. Provide the following electronically, with all formulae intact:
Provide all workpapers used and output files produced in the Reserve Margin Study.
Provide the Natural Gas Price forecast (in nominal dollars) that was used in that study.
Provide the derivation of the CT revenue requirements based on the economic carrying cost analysis used in the SERVM study, including a breakdown of all cost components included in the analysis.
Please identify any outside consultants (name of individual and the firm) who participated in the development of the Reserve Margin Study relied on in this IRP. For each such consultant, provide the area of responsibility or the work performed by such consultant on the Reserve Margin Study.
Please explain the extent to which gas or oil storage, and the use of dual fuel capable resources were modeled in the SERVM reserve margin analysis. Please identify all fossil fuel-fired generating units that were modeled that only had a single fuel source and explain why those resources do not have back-up fuel supplies.
In the 2022 IRP, Staff disagreed with the Company’s modeling of load forecast error in that the Company recentered the historical load forecast error distribution by subtracting the median percentage forecast error from the actual forecast error for each year. Has the Company continued to rely on this modeling approach or has the Company revised the modeling approach? If the Company has continued to rely on that modeling approach, please explain why, and if the Company has revised the modeling approach, please explain how the new approach was performed.
Response: 
All workpapers and output files from the Reserve Margin Study were provided to Commission Staff on January 31, 2025.
Please see STF-JKA-1-4 Attachment A TRADE SECRET.
The economic carrying cost (“ECC”) of a combustion turbine (“CT”) is not used directly in the SERVM model but instead is used to represent the cost of capacity as part of the economic optimum reserve margin (“EORM”) analysis. The workpaper, “Section V. B2024 CT ECC for RMS (TS).xlsx,” provided to Commission Staff in the Technical Appendix Volume 1 – Reserve Margin Study – I. Assumptions workpapers folder, details the components of the CT ECC.     
Astrapé Consulting’s services were used to update the Company’s First Tier (neighbor) data used to simulate market and emergency transactions as well as the Company’s solar weather year, hydro, and operating reserve demand curve (“ORDC”) data. Kevin Carden was the main contact for the engagement, and Astrapé Consulting has since merged with PowerGEM, LLC.
Oil storage was modeled for all existing dual fuel capable resources included in the study based on actual tank sizes. The incremental reserve margin dual fuel resources were modeled with unlimited fuel. Gas storage was not modeled as the study assumes the natural gas commodity is available to fully utilize the available pipeline capacity assigned to each resource. See STF-JKA-1-4 Attachment B for a list of modeled fossil fuel resources that do not have backup fuel supplies.
The Company has changed the methodology used to derive the load forecast error. The new methodology is no longer based on historical forecast data, but instead relies on a combination of model error and economic input uncertainty. The resulting distribution was not re-centered for the 2024 Reserve Margin Study. See Part G of Section I of the 2024 Reserve Margin Study provided in Technical Appendix Volume 1 for a detailed explanation of the new load forecast error methodology.


===== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-JKA-1 PD/STF-JKA-1-5.docx =====
STF-JKA-1-5

Question:
Modeling studies used in the IRP.
Please supply a list of all supply-side related modeling studies performed in the IRP (including the retirement study, environmental analyses, generation mix study, reserve margin study, etc.), Identify the associated models used in each of those studies (for example, Aurora, Genval, SERVM, REVREQ, Company spreadsheet models, etc.), and provide a brief description of each study that was performed.
Please provide all databases and workpapers for all supply-side-related models that were used in this IRP. Please provide an index or “table of contents” that describes each study performed.
Response: 
Supply-side Modeling Studies Performed:
Reserve Margin Study: The Reserve Margin Study report describes the methodology, metrics, assumptions, and results used to determine the Company’s Target Reserve Margin recommendations. The Reserve Margin Study was performed using SERVM.
Unit Retirement Study: The unit retirement studies were performed using a Company spreadsheet model used for asset evaluation and Aurora. The evaluations weigh the costs and benefits of continuing to operate coal and certain gas-steam units beyond 2028, including assessing the potential impact of various environmental compliance pathways.  Evaluations were performed for Plant Bowen Units 1-4, Plant Scherer Units 1-3, and Plant Gaston Units 1-4 & A. 
Unit Upgrade Analyses: The unit upgrade analyses were performed using a Company spreadsheet model used for asset evaluation and Aurora. The unit upgrade analyses compare the costs and benefits of continued operation of relevant units with upgrades and without upgrades. Evaluations were performed for Plant McIntosh Units 1A-8A, Plant McIntosh Units 10-11, Plant Vogtle Units 1-2, and Plant Hatch Units 1-2. 
Wholesale-to-Retail offer: The Wholesale-to-Retail offer was performed using a Company spreadsheet model. The market differential adjustment (“MDA”) assessment was performed to determine the difference between the levelized market value and the levelized revenue requirement of the net asset over its assumed remaining life.  
Hydro Modernization Study: The hydro modernization study was performed using a Company spreadsheet model used for asset evaluation and Aurora. The hydro modernization study compares the costs and benefits of modernization to the costs and benefits of alternatives to modernization. Evaluations were performed for Plant Tallulah, Plant Yonah, Plant Bartletts Ferry Units 5-6, Plant Goat Rock, Plant North Highlands, Plant Lloyd Shoals, Plant Wallace, Plant Flint River, and Plant Morgan Falls. An evaluation for Plant Burton was also performed per Paragraph 34 in the 2022 Final Order Adopting Stipulation. 
Renewable Integration Study: The Renewable Integration Study evaluated the reliability and cost impacts of large solar penetration levels. The study was performed by Astrape Consulting utilizing SERVM.
Resource Mix Study: A Resource Mix Study with nine scenarios was performed using Aurora. The Resource Mix Study aims to develop an optimal, least-cost resource mix or generic expansion plan. This plan is designed to minimize revenue requirements while adhering to reliability criteria and environmental laws and regulations. It also takes into account risk and flexibility, providing a valuable roadmap for long-term resource decision-making.
DSM Step 9 Analysis:  The Commission-approved nine-step DSM Planning Process, or “DSM Program Planning Approach,” was used to guide the development of the Company’s 2025 IRP and DSM Certification plans.
Financial Review:  A Financial Review of thirteen Sensitivities was performed using Aurora. Details and results of the financial review can be found in the Technical Appendix Volume 2, Section 3.
Supply-Side Modeling Workpapers:
The Company provided databases and workpapers to Commission Staff on January 31, 2025, complete with a workpapers index.
Reserve Margin Study: Workpapers were provided in the Technical Appendix Volume 1 – Reserve Margin Study workpapers folder.
Unit Retirement Studies: Workpapers were provided in the Technical Appendix Volume 1 – Unit Retirement Study workpapers folder.
Unit Upgrade Analyses: Workpapers were provided in the Technical Appendix Volume 1 – Unit Upgrade Analyses workpapers folder.
Wholesale-to-Retail offer: Workpapers were provided in the Technical Appendix Volume 1 – Wholesale-to-Retail Offer workpapers folder.
Hydro Modernization Study: Workpapers were provided in the Technical Appendix Volume 1 – Hydro Modernization workpapers folder.
Renewable Integration Study: Workpapers were provided in the Technical Appendix Volume 2 – Renewable Integration Study workpapers folder.

DSM Step 9 Analysis: Workpapers, databases, and Aurora modeling file index were provided in the Technical Appendix Volume 1 – DSM Program Documentation workpapers folder.
Financial Review: Workpapers, databases, and Aurora modeling file index were provided in the Technical Appendix Volume 2 – Resource Mix Study workpapers folder.

Aurora databases, workpapers, run setups, and a workpapers index were provided to Commission Staff on January 31, 2025. Additionally, Aurora databases and workpapers accompanying an Errata associated with the 111-MG0 Supply-Side DSM case were provided to Commission Staff on February 14, 2025. See response to subpart (a).
See response to subpart (a).
The Company has no record of initialization errors. There may be instances where Aurora issues a warning upon initialization. Generally, each warning is unique and is investigated based on the message and how it relates to the given study. 
Please see Table 4 of Section 3.6.1 “Expansion Plan Candidate Resources” in the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix Vol 2 Resource Mix Study for a detailed description of new resource constraints included in Aurora modeling. Please also see Table 5 of Section 3.6.2 “Generic Unit Costs and Performance” in the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix Vol 2 Resource Mix Study for a list of Effective Load Carrying Capability (“ELCC”) values applied for each technology. Additionally, please see the response to STF-JKA-1-10 for detailed information on the development of these ELCC values used in Aurora. All constraints modeled in Aurora are an attempt to model and simulate the operations and economic planning of Southern Company’s electric generation system. These constraints are often provided and modeled from input from Bulk Power and Commercial Operations. Must run constraints are largely directed by modeling Bulk Power, Transmission Planning, and Commercial Operations’ guidance for the system.
Yes, the Company included capacity factor limitations in its modeling. Please see Section 3.6.1 “Expansion Plan Candidate Resources” in the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix Vol. 2 Resource Mix Study for information regarding capacity factor limits under the 111 view. Also listed in Section 3.6.1 is the Company’s use of a capacity factor limit on combustion turbines (“CTs”), which applies to both new and existing CTs as a group. This capacity factor limit is broadly applied to CTs to reflect existing requirements under the Clean Air Act’s New Source Performance Standards (“NSPS”) Subpart TTTT as well as existing and potential air permit limitations. Under the NSPS regulation, new simple-cycle CTs must meet a capacity factor limitation that is equivalent to the unit’s design efficiency. In addition, simple-cycle CTs could be required to limit capacity factor due to New Source Review air permit limitations under the Clean Air Act. While air permit constraints are determined on a case-by-case basis, many existing air permits limit simple-cycle CTs to a 20% annual capacity factor or less. Simple-cycle CTs are generally used as peaking generation and have historically operated at far less than a 20% capacity factor on an annual basis.

===== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-JKA-1 PD/STF-JKA-1-8.docx =====
STF-JKA-1-8

Question:  
Provide source documents for any capital cost escalation rates that were modeled.

Response:

All technologies except for wind, solar, and battery storage are escalated at the rate of the Gross Domestic Product Implicit Price Deflator (“GPDIPD”). Please refer to attachment JKA-1-8 Attachment A TRADE SECRET for development of the Implicit Price Deflator used to model generic units in the Resource Mix Study.
Escalators for solar and battery storage, as represented in Figure 12 of the Resource Mix Study in Technical Appendix Volume 2, were developed using capex forecast data from the “1Q 2024 Global PV Market Outlook” from Bloomberg New Energy Finance (“BNEF”). The escalator for wind is based on similar data from the “2024 v1 Annual Technology Baseline” (“ATB”) from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (“NREL”). The calculation of these escalation rates begins with the overnight capital cost forecasts for each technology from the most recent BNEF Levelized Cost of Energy (“LCOE”) spreadsheet that can be accessed by BNEF clients. When these escalation trajectories were established, the most recent BNEF LCOE publication was the “Energy Storage System Cost Survey 2023.” Solar PV was informed by BNEF while wind was informed by the ATB. The forecasted values published by BNEF were originally in 2023 dollars. To be consistent with other costs included in the Resource Mix Study, nominal values were calculated for this forecast by escalating each year’s projection in real terms using the Company’s forecast of the GDPIPD. The final step normalizes the forecasted trajectories so that the capital cost changes can be applied to the Company’s most recent overnight cost estimate in the first year of the forecast. The normalization calculation divides the nominal capital cost projection for all future years by the overnight cost estimate in year one. The normalized capital escalation trajectories for onshore wind, solar PV and battery energy storage are included in the “Mix Study - Figure 12 Normalized Wind Solar BESS Projections TRADE SECRET.xlsx” workpaper provided to Commission Staff on January 31, 2025, in the Technical Appendix Vol 2 – Resource Mix Study workpapers folder. Development of the chart provided in the workpaper is detailed in STF-JKA-1-8 Attachment B TRADE SECRET.
The Company uses the BNEF capital cost forecasts included in its LCOE publications because it is driven by extensive data collection and quantitative learning curve analysis by BNEF as described in the Methodology section of the Energy Storage System Cost Survey 2023, which is accessible to BNEF clients.
 

===== DKT 56002 & 56003 STF-JKA-1 PD/STF-JKA-1-9.docx =====
STF-JKA-1-9

Question:
For a number of years, the Company has taken steps to mitigate risks of cold weather reliability. Please describe all efforts undertaken since the 2022 IRP including capital investment and O&M expense, and explain how those steps have paid off, and how the Company’s Aurora and SERVM modeling assumptions have been revised since the 2022 IRP as a result of the mitigation efforts undertaken.

Response:

Since the 2022 IRP, cold weather outage assumptions in the model have been adjusted to account for the ongoing winterization improvements performed across the System. In the 2021 Reserve Margin Study, incremental cold weather-related outages for all modeled resources were anticipated to start when system-weighted temperatures fell below 13°F. In the 2024 Reserve Margin Study, this threshold was adjusted downward to 10°F but only for retail resources owned and operated by Southern Company. For contracted resources, the threshold was increased to 18°F due to fewer winterization improvements being performed on these units. In addition to the threshold, a geographic adjustment was also made at each generation site to account for differences between local temperature and the system-weighted temperature. Part I, Section I of the 2024 Reserve Margin Study provided in Technical Appendix Volume 1 details the cold weather outage modeling methodology and assumptions applied. The Aurora modeling for the Resource Mix Study applies the target reserve margin determined in the Reserve Margin Study to help identify an optimized resource expansion plan. Loads modeled in the Resource Mix Study are based on normal weather, so no incremental extreme weather outages are applied.
Southern Company is currently implementing a fleetwide winterization program with the goal of not only improving the reliability of freeze protection systems at each plant but also lowering the minimum operating temperature and freeze related parameters. This includes adding/replacing various components such as heat tracing, insulation, instrument enclosures, heated tube bundles, equipment enclosures, and other auxiliaries related to protecting components during cold weather events. Procedures have also been updated to assure compliance with NERC EOP-012-2 Extreme Cold Weather Preparedness. To date, Georgia Power has invested over $100M capital and over $7M O&M in this effort. As a result, the Georgia Power fleet winter reliability continues to improve. No unplanned generation weather related events were experienced for Company owned resources during Winter Storms Enzo and Cora.
